passage_text: Researchers studied the effects of a novel dietary supplement on resting metabolic rate (RMR) in healthy adults. The study recruited 90 participants, randomly assigned to three groups: Group A received the supplement, Group B received a placebo, and Group C received no intervention. After a 4‑week intervention period, RMR was measured using indirect calorimetry. The data are summarized in Table 1. The researchers reported that Group A had a mean RMR of 6.1 kcal/min (SD = 0.8, N = 30), Group B had a mean RMR of 5.2 kcal/min (SD = 0.9, N = 30), and Group C had a mean RMR of 4.9 kcal/min (SD = 0.7, N = 30). The authors concluded that the supplement increased RMR compared to placebo and no‑intervention controls.
stem: Which sample shows the greatest variability?
explanation: Correct: B) Sample B has the largest SD (0.9) and also the largest coefficient of variation (0.9/5.2 = 17%, versus 13% for A and 14% for C). Why the others are wrong: A) Sample A has SD 0.8, less than B, though it has the highest mean. C) Sample C has the smallest SD (0.7). D) The SDs of 0.7 to 0.9 are not identical, and B is highest.
trap: Students often assume that the sample with the largest mean has the greatest variability.

stem: Which statistical test would best test whether the difference between Sample A and Sample B is significant?
explanation: Correct: Groups A and B are different, independent groups of 30 participants, so their means are compared with an independent-samples t-test. Why the others are wrong: A) a one-sample t-test compares one mean with a fixed value. C) a paired t-test needs the same participants measured twice. D) chi-square tests compare categorical counts, not means.
trap: Choosing a paired t‑test assumes the same participants were measured twice, which is not the case.

stem: Calculate the Cohen’s d effect size for the difference between Sample A and Sample B.
explanation: Pooled SD = √[(0.8² + 0.9²)/2] ≈ 0.851; mean difference = 0.9; Cohen’s d = 0.9/0.851 ≈ 1.06.
trap: Students often use the larger SD instead of the pooled SD, yielding an underestimate of the effect size.

stem: Which of the following is a common mistake when interpreting the results of this study?

options.A: Concluding the effect is clinically important from statistical significance alone, without considering effect size and variability

explanation: A p-value does not indicate the practical size or importance of an effect; effect size, variability and clinical relevance must also be considered. Using a large sample, reporting means and calculating SDs are standard good practice.
trap: Treating a significant p-value as proof of a large, clinically meaningful effect.

stem: Which comparison best isolates the effect of the supplement itself from the effect of receiving a pill-like treatment?

options.D: Group C versus its own baseline

explanation: Correct: A) Groups A and B differ only in receiving the supplement or the placebo, so A versus B isolates the supplement (6.1 versus 5.2 kcal/min). Why the others are wrong: B) Group C received nothing, so A versus C mixes the supplement with the effect of receiving any treatment. C) B versus C estimates the placebo effect only. D) No baseline values were reported for Group C.
trap: Comparing the supplement group with the no-intervention group, which mixes the supplement effect with any effect of simply receiving a treatment.
